name: autoreview
description: Joel-adapted closeout code review loop. Use when the user asks for autoreview, Codex review, Claude/second-model review, local branch review, PR review, final review before commit/ship, or after risky non-trivial code edits when an external reviewer is worth the spend.
basis: https://github.com/openclaw/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/autoreview/SKILL.md plus local code-review-clis/session receipts
---

# Auto Review

Run a closeout review loop against real diffs. This is advisory code review, not approval routing and not an excuse to outsource judgment.

## Local Contract

- Do not run autoreview while a pi-codex-goal objective is actively auto-continuing. The goal package and review commands both use follow-up turns; with Pi `followUpMode: all`, combining them can corrupt Codex tool-call ordering (`No tool call found for function call output`). Pause or complete the goal first, then run review.
- Inspect `git status --short` and identify the diff scope before invoking a reviewer.
- Preserve user work. Do not patch unrelated dirty files or reset the checkout.
- Treat reviewer output as claims. Verify every accepted finding by reading the actual code path and adjacent files.
- Reject speculative edge cases, broad rewrites, style churn, and fixes that complicate the ownership boundary without killing a real bug.
- Prefer the smallest correct patch at the right boundary.
- If a review-triggered fix changes code, rerun focused tests and rerun the relevant review path when the risk justifies it.
- Do not push just to review. Push only when Joel asked to push/ship/update a PR.
- Do not use remote review APIs for secrets, raw transcripts, customer private data, paid corpus, or machine overlays.

## Pick Target

Start with local receipts:

```sh
git status --short
git diff --stat
git diff --cached --stat
git branch --show-current
```

Dirty local work:

```sh
codex exec review --uncommitted
```

Branch or PR work:

```sh
base=$(gh pr view --json baseRefName --jq .baseRefName 2>/dev/null || printf 'main')
codex exec review --base "origin/$base"
```

Committed single change:

```sh
codex exec review --commit HEAD
```

Use commit review for already-landed or already-pushed work on `main`. Reviewing a clean `main` checkout against `origin/main` usually proves nothing useful.

## Local Reviewer Stack

This machine has three useful closeout review paths:

1. Codex review for the default structured closeout loop.
2. Macroscope for local isolated review and autoloop-style review.
3. CodeRabbit CLI for agent-readable CodeRabbit review when Joel asks for it or a repo expects it.

Default to Codex review when Joel asks for `autoreview`, `Codex review`, or a generic closeout review:

```sh
codex exec review --uncommitted
codex exec review --base origin/main
codex exec review --commit HEAD
```

Use Macroscope when Joel asks for Macroscope, local isolated review, or autoloop-style review:

```sh
command -v macroscope
macroscope codereview
```

Use CodeRabbit when Joel asks for CodeRabbit, asks for an agent-readable external review, or the repo workflow expects it. It sends review context to CodeRabbit:

```sh
command -v coderabbit || command -v cr
coderabbit doctor
coderabbit review --agent
```

If Joel asks for Manifold:

```sh
command -v manifold
```

If unavailable, say so. Do not silently substitute another reviewer.

If Joel asks for a Claude or second-model review and no structured helper is installed, run the requested reviewer directly with a tight prompt and the frozen diff context. Keep the main agent responsible for validating claims.

## Closeout Loop

1. Format first if formatting can change line locations.
2. Run focused tests before review when tests are cheap and likely to catch churn.
3. Run the chosen review command against the correct target.
4. Triage reviewer findings into accepted, rejected, and deferred.
5. Verify accepted findings against real files before editing.
6. Patch accepted findings only.
7. Rerun focused tests after fixes.
8. Rerun review only when code changed in response to review or the original risk is high enough to justify the spend.
9. Stop when the final review command is clean or when remaining findings are consciously rejected with a short reason.

Do not run extra review cycles just to get prettier closeout wording.

## Long-Running Reviews

Reviewers can be slow. Treat progress lines or steady process activity as healthy. Do not kill a review just because it is quiet for a few minutes. Check the process only after an obvious subprocess failure, missing progress for a long window, or a run that is clearly beyond the expected review duration.

## Relationship To Other Skills

- `code-review-clis` owns tool-specific Macroscope, CodeRabbit, Manifold, and Hunk safety details.
- `tdd` owns test-first feature work.
- `diagnose` owns hard bug diagnosis before review.
- `session-search` is useful when a review question depends on prior agent context or a repeated local workflow decision.

## Final Report

Include:

- review command used
- tests or proof run
- accepted findings and fixes applied
- rejected findings with brief reasons
- final clean result, or the conscious reason a remaining finding was not fixed

Keep the report short. The useful thing is the decision trail, not reviewer fan fiction.

# Brain Teach

Teach inside the current repo's `.brain/`, not a throwaway chat. The point is demonstrated understanding that future sessions can reuse.

Source credit: this skill adapts `alexknowshtml`'s `/teach` skill, which credits Suzanne's Anthropic "Learn Quiz" prompt shared by `@trq212`. Keep the good part: Socratic mastery, one concept at a time, and a checklist that only completes when understanding is demonstrated. Replace the Claude-only parts with Joel's stack: Pi/Claude/Codex session search, `.brain/`, pi-notes, and explicit commit approval.

## What makes this ours

- Brain is the learning workspace. `sessions/teaching/*.md` is not the default.
- Session sources come from Pi/Claude/Codex receipts via `session_search`, `session_chunks`, `session_context`, or bounded local transcript reads, not only `~/.claude/projects` grep.
- Teaching is source-grounded. Read the file, transcript, code, notes, docs, logs, or diff before claiming what happened.
- No auto commit/push. Update files, run checks, report paths. Commit only when Joel explicitly asks, and use the configured GitHub actor rules.
- Use short, sharp questions. Do not turn teaching into a fuckin syllabus unless the mission needs one.

## Modes

### Session mastery mode

Use when Joel asks `/teach`, "teach me what happened", "quiz me on that session", "help me understand this change", or provides a session/topic/file.

Goal: turn a real source into concrete concepts, quiz one at a time, and update a Brain checklist after every confirmed item.

### Topic learning path mode

Use when Joel wants to learn a broader topic over time.

Goal: create or update a small Brain project with mission, sources, glossary, current edge, next lesson, and learning records.

### Teaching-someone-else mode

Use when Joel says `--student <name>`, "help me teach Kristina", "help me teach someone else", or asks for a walkthrough guide.

Goal: help Joel teach the concept. Progress tracks what Joel has explicitly covered and confirmed the student understands.

## Source resolution

Before teaching, resolve the source of truth.

1. **File path**: read the file directly. Supports session JSONL, `.md`, `.svx`, diffs, PRDs, plans, and notes.
2. **Session/topic query**: use the session-search skill/tooling when available:
   - `session_search` for pointers across Pi, Claude, and Codex
   - `session_chunks` for tight transcript context
   - `session_context` or `session_inspect` when exact receipts matter
3. **Current repo change**: inspect `git diff`, relevant files, tests, logs, and Brain notes before teaching.
4. **External factual topic**: read primary docs/sources first. If sources are missing, create a sources note with a `Gaps` section before teaching.
5. **No argument**: ask one quick setup question: current session, recent session/topic, file path, or broader topic?

Do not paste raw transcripts, secrets, customer data, paid source text, or private overlays into the teaching note. Store source pointers and concise receipts.

## Brain workspace

Use project-local `.brain/` first. If the topic is machine/operator-wide rather than project-local, use `/Users/joel/.brain`.

Ask: **where will this be useful next?** Place notes by future use, not topic vibes.

Preferred files:

- `.brain/projects/<topic>-learning-path.svx` — mission, success criteria, constraints, current edge, next lesson, and completion condition.
- `.brain/resources/<topic>-sources.svx` — trusted knowledge sources and practitioners/communities.
- `.brain/resources/<topic>-glossary.svx` — compressed terminology Joel has demonstrated he understands.
- `.brain/resources/teaching-checklists/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.svx` — session mastery checklist.
- `.brain/resources/learning-records/<topic>/<nnnn>-<slug>.svx` — durable evidence of demonstrated understanding, corrected misconceptions, or mission shifts.
- `.brain/resources/tutorials/<topic>-<lesson>.svx` — source-grounded reusable lesson/explainer notes.
- `.brain/components` / `.brain/data` — optional pi-notes components or data-backed explainers when static prose is weak.

## Session mastery checklist

Create the checklist after source resolution and before quizzing.

Use this shape for `.brain/resources/teaching-checklists/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.svx`:

```md
---
title: "Teaching: {Session or Topic Title}"
type: "resource"
status: "active"
created_at: "YYYY-MM-DD"
tags:
  - teaching-checklist
  - learning
  - {topic}
mode: "solo | teaching"
student: "{name, if teaching mode}"
source: "{topic, file path, session id, or URL}"
---

# Teaching: {Session or Topic Title}

## Source receipts

- {file path, session id, URL, command, or note link}

## Progress

0/{total} concepts confirmed

## The Problem

- [ ] {specific item}
- [ ] {why the problem existed}
- [ ] {branch, tradeoff, or alternative considered}

## The Solution

- [ ] {how it was resolved}
- [ ] {why this approach over others}
- [ ] {key decision}
- [ ] {edge case or failure mode handled}

## Broader Context

- [ ] {what this impacts}
- [ ] {why it matters later}
- [ ] {what to watch for next}

---
_Last updated: YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm TZ_
```

Extract concrete items from the source. No generic placeholders like "understand architecture". If the source is thin, say so and ask for the missing source instead of inventing concepts.

## Topic learning path notes

Use this shape for `.brain/projects/<topic>-learning-path.svx`:

```md
---
title: "{Topic} Learning Path"
type: "project"
status: "active"
created_at: "YYYY-MM-DD"
tags:
  - learning
  - {topic}
---

# {Topic} Learning Path

## Mission

{1-3 sentences. The concrete real-world goal. Avoid "understand X" unless the real outcome is explicit.}

## Success looks like

- {Specific observable capability}
- {Specific observable output or decision Joel can make}

## Constraints

- {Time, budget, source limits, learning preferences, project constraints}

## Out of scope

- {Adjacent rabbit holes to avoid for now}

## Current edge

{What Joel already knows, what is just beyond reach, and what lesson/exercise comes next. Link learning records.}

## Next lesson

{The smallest useful lesson tied to the mission.}

## Links

- Sources: [[../resources/{topic}-sources]]
- Glossary: [[../resources/{topic}-glossary]]
- Learning records: [[../resources/learning-records/{topic}/index]]
```

Keep it short. If it grows past a screen, split planning detail into linked notes.

## Sources note

Use this shape for `.brain/resources/<topic>-sources.svx`:

```md
---
title: "{Topic} Sources"
type: "resource"
status: "active"
created_at: "YYYY-MM-DD"
tags:
  - learning
  - sources
  - {topic}
---

# {Topic} Sources

## Knowledge

- [{Source title}]({url-or-local-path})
  Covers: {what it is good for}. Use when: {lesson/question type}.

## Wisdom / Practitioners / Communities

- [{Community or practitioner}]({url-or-local-path})
  Use when: {where real-world judgment or feedback is needed}.

## Gaps

- {Missing source needed before teaching a subtopic}
```

Prefer primary docs, source code, peer-reviewed material, recognized practitioners, and high-signal communities. Prune shallow sources.

## Glossary note

Use this shape for `.brain/resources/<topic>-glossary.svx`:

```md
---
title: "{Topic} Glossary"
type: "resource"
status: "active"
created_at: "YYYY-MM-DD"
tags:
  - learning
  - glossary
  - {topic}
---

# {Topic} Glossary

One sentence describing the topic language this glossary governs.

## Terms

**Term**: Tight definition in one or two sentences.
_Avoid_: fuzzy synonym, overloaded phrase
```

Only add a term after Joel demonstrates understanding. The glossary is compressed knowledge, not a pre-reading dictionary.

## Learning records

Create records lazily under `.brain/resources/learning-records/<topic>/`.

Use one record when Joel:

- demonstrates real understanding of a non-trivial concept
- states prior knowledge that should prevent re-teaching
- corrects a misconception
- changes the mission because of learning

Shape:

```md
---
title: "{Short learned thing}"
type: "resource"
status: "active"
created_at: "YYYY-MM-DD"
tags:
  - learning-record
  - {topic}
---

# {Short learned thing}

{1-3 sentences: what was learned or established, why it matters for future sessions, and evidence if useful.}
```

Do not create session logs. Coverage is not learning.

## Teaching loop

Every lesson should do this:

1. **Anchor** — tie the lesson to the mission, source, and current edge.
2. **Source** — cite the trusted source note or read the source before claiming facts.
3. **Ask first** — have Joel restate what he thinks happened or answer one targeted question.
4. **Explain** — fill the smallest gap; do not re-cover what he already has.
5. **Exercise** — ask Joel to apply it immediately.
6. **Feedback** — correct or deepen based on the answer/output.
7. **Capture** — update checklist/glossary/learning records only when there is evidence.
8. **Next edge** — name the next smallest useful lesson.

For session mastery, re-read the checklist file before each exchange, pick the next unchecked item, and ask exactly one question.

Rules for quiz questions:

- One question at a time. No multipart sludge.
- Open-ended questions are best for mastery.
- Use multiple choice sparingly. In Pi, do not use the `mcq` tool for quiz answers because recommendations/preselects can leak the answer; use `mcq` only for setup/intent choices.
- If Joel is correct, mark `[x]` immediately, update progress inline, then move on.
- If Joel misses, explain briefly and re-ask in a different form before marking confirmed.
- Every 3-4 exchanges, show checklist progress.
- Never offer to wrap up until every item is `[x]` or Joel explicitly stops the learning run.

## Teaching-someone-else loop

For `--student <name>` or teach-someone-else requests:

1. Use the same source resolution and checklist.
2. Reframe each item as: how Joel should explain it, what example to use, and what one question confirms understanding.
3. Progress tracks items Joel says he covered and confirmed.
4. Keep private/internal context out of student-facing phrasing unless Joel approves sharing it.

## Pi-notes checks

After changing `.brain/` notes or components, run the best available Brain check:

```bash
pi-notes brain check
```

If the local command is unavailable, use the `pi_notes_brain_check` tool when present. Open rendered notes in the Document Host when visual truth matters.

## Output shape

When starting:

- Source receipt(s)
- Checklist path or learning path path
- First question

During:

- One question or one correction
- Progress count after confirmed items
- Path touched when the checklist changes

When complete:

- Completed checklist path
- Any glossary/learning-record paths created
- Checks run
- Commit/push status
- Next edge, if useful

## Rules

- Source first. If sources are missing, create a `Gaps` section and search/read before teaching.
- Keep the zone tight. One useful edge beats a broad syllabus.
- Use Brain links and backlinks so future sessions can resume.
- Do not leak private sources, paid corpus text, secrets, transcripts, or customer data.
- Do not pretend the user learned something because it was explained. Require evidence.
- Do not build a platform. Edit the living Brain notes.

# Caveman

Respond terse like smart caveman. Substance stay. Fluff die.

## Persistence

Active every response once triggered. No drift back. Off only when user says `stop caveman` or `normal mode`.

## Rules

Drop:

- filler
- pleasantries
- hedging
- corporate sludge
- over-explaining

Keep:

- exact technical terms
- exact errors
- file paths
- commands
- warnings for destructive actions
- receipts
- `.svx` frontmatter and code blocks unchanged

Pattern:

```txt
[thing] [action] -> [reason]. Next: [step].
```

Examples:

```txt
Auth bug. Expiry check uses `<` not `<=`. Fix middleware, add boundary test.
```

```txt
Pool = reuse DB conn. Skip handshake -> faster under load.
```

## Auto-Clarity Exception

Temporarily stop caveman for:

- destructive action confirmations
- security/privacy warnings
- customer-facing copy
- multi-step instructions where fragments risk misread
- when Joel asks for clarification

Resume after clear part done.

## Brain / SVX

Caveman changes prose style, not artifact correctness. If writing Brain notes, keep valid `.svx` frontmatter, headings, links, receipts, and `pi-notes brain check` discipline.

# Code Review CLIs

Use local reviewer tools as advisors, not as patch gods.

For a full closeout loop with target selection, tests, review, fix, and final
reporting, use the `autoreview` skill. This skill owns the tool-specific safety
details.

## Receipts first

Before running a review:

- inspect `git status --short`
- identify the diff scope
- avoid sending secrets or private data to remote review APIs
- preserve user work; do not patch unrelated dirty files

## Hunk

Hunk is installed at `/opt/homebrew/bin/hunk` and configured as the global Git difftool.

- Do not launch interactive `hunk diff` / `git difftool` unless Joel asks for an interactive diff viewer.
- If an existing Hunk window matters, use `hunk session ...` commands instead of guessing from memory.

## Macroscope

Use for local review/autoloop requests.

- Check availability first: `command -v macroscope`.
- Default command: `macroscope codereview`.
- It creates an isolated review worktree by default.
- Do not patch the user's original working tree unless Joel explicitly asks for autoloop or direct fixes.

## CodeRabbit

Use for CodeRabbit reviews only when Joel asks or the repo workflow expects it.

- Check availability/auth first: `command -v coderabbit || command -v cr`.
- Preferred command: `coderabbit review --agent` or `cr review --agent`.
- Remember diffs are sent to CodeRabbit's API; avoid reviewing secrets.

## Manifold

If Joel asks for Manifold review:

```sh
command -v manifold
```

If unavailable, say so. Do not pretend or substitute another reviewer silently.

## Handling reviewer output

- Validate each finding against real code before fixing.
- Prefer the smallest correct patch.
- Run the narrowest useful verification after changes.
- In the operator summary, separate: reviewer claims, validated issues, fixes applied, checks run, and leftovers.

name: diagnose
description: Disciplined diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Reproduce → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → regression-test. Use when user says "diagnose this" / "debug this", reports a bug, says something is broken/throwing/failing, or describes a performance regression.
basis: /Users/joel/Code/mattpocock/skills/skills/engineering/diagnose
---

# Diagnose

Start with Matt's feedback-loop discipline, then add local receipts: Brain, pi-notes, session history, logs, and harness state.

## Receipt First

Before hypothesizing, identify the failing surface:

- user-visible behavior
- command/test output
- logs/trace/event IDs
- changed files/commits/config
- harness: Codex, Claude, OpenCode, Pi, dark-wizard, Panda, gateway, k8s, Vercel

If prior context may matter, search sessions:

```sh
joelclaw sessions search "<symptom or project>" --source both --machine dark-wizard --limit 5 --extract
```

If the issue is project/process level, inspect project `.brain/**/*.svx` through pi-notes when present, plus `~/.brain` for cross-project/operator context, before changing code. Treat `BRAIN.md`/`CONTEXT.md` as legacy evidence only.

## Phase 1 — Build The Loop

Create the fastest honest pass/fail signal:

1. failing unit/integration/e2e test
2. CLI command or curl script
3. Playwright/browser repro
4. captured payload/event replay
5. log query or Axiom/gateway trace
6. raw Pi/session replay or inspection
7. HITL checklist only when automation is impossible

No loop means no confident fix. Say what was tried and what artifact is needed.

## Phase 2 — Reproduce

Run the loop. Confirm the failure mode is the user's bug, not adjacent smoke.

For nondeterministic bugs, raise the reproduction rate with stress, repeats, parallelism, sleeps, seeded data, or narrower timing windows.

## Phase 3 — Hypothesize

Write 3-5 ranked, falsifiable hypotheses. For each:

- prediction
- probe
- expected confirming result
- expected falsifying result

Proceed with the best probe unless Joel is actively steering and needs to re-rank.

## Phase 4 — Instrument

Each probe maps to one prediction. Change one variable at a time.

Use debugger/REPL first when available, then targeted logs. Tag temporary logs with a unique prefix like `[DEBUG-a4f2]` so cleanup is grep-able.

For perf regressions, measure/bisect instead of logging vibes.

## Phase 5 — Fix + Regression Test

Add a regression test at the real seam when possible. If no good seam exists, document that architecture finding.

After the fix:

- run the narrow regression test
- re-run the original feedback loop
- remove debug instrumentation
- clean throwaway harnesses/prototypes

## SVX Capture

When diagnosis reveals reusable truth, update the right durable surface:

- project `.brain/projects/<slug>.svx` for active incident/bug project state
- `.brain/resources/<bug-class-or-system>.svx` for reusable findings
- `.brain/resources/decisions/<slug>.svx` or repo ADR for hard-to-reverse fixes/constraints
- skill/runbook docs when future agents need the rule

Capture symptom, loop, winning hypothesis, fix, validation, and prevention. Do not dump raw logs, secrets, customer data, or transcripts. Run `pi-notes brain check .` after Brain edits when available.

name: empirical-subagents
description: "Use alongside pi-subagents when launching parallel subagents, fan-out/fan-in, parallel research, parallel context-build, review fanout, validators, or any workflow where branches should gather real-world experience before synthesis. Triggers on 'fan-out fan-in', 'parallel experience', 'empirical fanout', 'accumulate experience', 'back-pressure', 'subagent branches', and improving subagent usage."
---

# Empirical Subagents

Use this with `pi-subagents` when parallelism should create better contact with reality, not just more tokens.

## Core rule

Fan-out is valuable when each branch accumulates different **experience** and fan-in compresses that experience into learnings.

A branch has experience when theory meets a back-pressure surface:

- tests or commands;
- real source docs or source code;
- local files, call paths, configs, fixtures, and tests;
- logs, API responses, DB rows, traces, screenshots;
- browser/user-flow interaction;
- prototype spikes, benchmarks, or counterexample searches.

If branches only answer the same prompt from vibes, call it parallel opinion and lower confidence.

## Parent orchestration pattern

1. Frame one shared question or decision.
2. Pick two to four branches with distinct reality surfaces.
3. Give each branch an experience contract.
4. Keep writes single-threaded unless explicitly using isolated worktrees.
5. Synthesize contradictions and learnings before deciding.

Use fresh context for independent observation. Use forked context only when inherited history is the point, such as drift audits or oracle-style trajectory review.

## Branch experience contract

Each branch prompt should include:

- **Angle / hypothesis**: what this branch is trying to learn.
- **Back-pressure surface**: what it must inspect or exercise.
- **Receipts**: file ranges, command output, screenshots, links, rows, logs, traces, exact errors, or reproduction notes.
- **Useful negative result**: what failed search, non-repro, or dead end would still teach us.
- **Output**: observations, changed beliefs, confidence, gaps, and decision implication.

## Fan-in synthesis contract

The parent or synthesis `context-builder` should return:

- condensed learnings that survived fan-in;
- strongest receipts;
- contradictions and likely explanations;
- weak branches that reasoned without enough observation;
- decision rules or recommended approach;
- next experiment, implementation step, or user question.

Do not average summaries. Fan-in is compression, conflict resolution, and next-action selection.

## Prompt shape

```text
Goal: answer/decide ...

Experience contract:
- Angle/hypothesis: ...
- Back-pressure surface: inspect/run/check ...
- Required receipts: ...
- Useful negative result: ...

Return:
- What you inspected or ran
- Receipts
- Observations
- What changed from first impressions
- Negative findings/dead ends
- Confidence and gaps
- Decision implication or next experiment
```

## Good branch sets

- External docs/source + local code path + runtime reproduction.
- Correctness review + user-flow validator + simplicity/maintainability review.
- Log forensics + DB/API state + code path trace.
- Prior-art research + local architecture constraints + counterexample/security pass.

## Bad branch sets

- Three agents all asked “what do you think?”
- Reviewers that trust the worker summary instead of inspecting the diff.
- Researchers that summarize blogs without primary sources.
- Validators that report “looks good” without running or inspecting anything.

# Grill Me

Be a pressure tester, not a questionnaire bot.

The job is to find the fuzzy edge, ask the next question that matters, and keep going until the plan is executable or we discover it is bullshit.

## Before asking

Read what can be read:

- project `.brain/**/*.svx` through pi-notes when present, plus `~/.brain` for cross-project/operator context
- repo operating docs (`AGENTS.md`, `.pi/APPEND_SYSTEM.md`, README), docs, ADRs, and local instructions as evidence
- legacy context docs (`BRAIN.md`, `CONTEXT.md`, `CONTEXT-MAP.md`, `lat.md/`) only as migration/evidence sources
- relevant code/tests/config/logs
- prior project notes or session history when the topic has lineage

Use bounded session search only when prior agent context matters:

```sh
joelclaw sessions search "<topic>" --source both --machine dark-wizard --limit 5 --extract
```

If the plan touches Brain/PARA/JITPM, inspect existing Brain notes before grilling. Do not ask Joel to restate facts already sitting in the repo.

## Question format

Ask **one** question at a time:

```txt
Question: ...

My recommendation: ...

Why: ...
```

No MCQ unless Joel explicitly asks. Voice-friendly prose wins.

Good questions force a branch:

- “Who is the first real user/operator this must serve?”
- “What would make this project done enough to archive?”
- “What can we cut without killing the outcome?”
- “What evidence would convince us this worked?”
- “What state are we in when cancellation happens?”

Bad questions ask for essays, preferences, or vibes.

## Decision tree

Probe in this order unless the context points elsewhere:

1. **Outcome** — what changes in the world when this works?
2. **User/operator** — who experiences the pain or runs the system?
3. **Non-goals** — what tempting adjacent thing are we not doing?
4. **Constraints** — time, budget, public/private boundary, source limits, existing system shape.
5. **Lifecycle** — states, transitions, retries, cancellation, resumability, child processes, ownership.
6. **Validation** — what commands, screenshots, logs, tests, user flows, or Brain receipts prove done?
7. **Downscope** — smallest packet that creates value or reduces uncertainty.
8. **Durable capture** — what needs to live in Brain/ADR/issues after the decision crystallizes?

For lifecycle-heavy work, sketch an XState v5 machine instead of boolean soup:

```txt
states: idle → preparing → running → waiting_for_human → validating → complete
failure states: blocked | failed | cancelled
key events: start, approve, reject, retry, cancel, validate, archive
```

Keep it rough until the branch is settled.

## Brain capture

When a decision matters later, edit the durable surface immediately:

- active outcome/plan: `.brain/projects/<slug>.svx`
- ongoing standard/responsibility: `.brain/areas/<slug>.svx`
- reusable term/source/receipt: `.brain/resources/<slug>.svx`
- hard-to-reverse decision: `.brain/resources/decisions/<slug>.svx` or repo ADR

Use `.svx` with small frontmatter, plain Markdown first, and project-local components only when they already exist. Run `pi-notes brain check .` or `pi_notes_brain_check` after Brain edits when available. Do not extend `CONTEXT.md`-style files unless Joel explicitly asks.

## Stop rule

Stop grilling when these are explicit:

- next action or next packet
- acceptance criteria / validation evidence
- non-goals
- major constraints and risks
- lifecycle states if relevant
- where the durable decision lives

Then summarize the agreed invariants and recommend the next move. If the plan is still fuzzy after several branches, say what is missing instead of pretending we have a plan.

# Improve Codebase Architecture

Use Matt's deep-module framing, but ground it in this repo's actual domain, pi-notes Brain notes, ADRs, and agent history.

## Vocabulary

Use these terms consistently:

- **Module** — anything with an interface and implementation.
- **Interface** — everything callers must know: types, invariants, ordering, error modes, config, performance.
- **Implementation** — code inside the module.
- **Depth** — leverage at the interface: lots of behavior behind a small surface.
- **Seam** — where behavior can vary without editing in place.
- **Adapter** — concrete thing satisfying an interface at a seam.
- **Leverage** — what callers get from depth.
- **Locality** — change, bugs, knowledge, and verification concentrated in one place.

Avoid overloaded sludge like "boundary" unless the repo uses it deliberately.

## Explore First

Read:

- `.brain/**/*.svx` Project/Area/Resource/Decision notes first; use pi-notes to check/render them when available.
- `~/.brain/**/*.svx` for cross-project, personal, or machine/operator context.
- `AGENTS.md`, `.pi/APPEND_SYSTEM.md`, README, domain docs, and ADRs as instructions/evidence.
- legacy context docs (`BRAIN.md`, `CONTEXT.md`, `CONTEXT-MAP.md`, `lat.md/`) only as migration/evidence sources.
- relevant code and tests
- recent session friction when architecture was already discussed

```sh
joelclaw sessions search "<repo architecture topic>" --source both --machine dark-wizard --limit 5 --extract
```

Run `pi-notes brain check .` when Brain structure matters or after Brain edits.

## Find Real Friction

Look for:

- shallow modules that only move complexity around
- missing seams where bugs cannot be tested
- concepts with no stable domain name
- repeated agent confusion in prior sessions
- code paths where understanding requires bouncing across many tiny files
- architecture that contradicts a current Brain/ADR decision

Apply the deletion test: if deleting the module makes complexity vanish, it was probably pass-through. If complexity reappears across callers, the module earns its keep.

## Present Candidates

For each candidate:

- files/modules involved
- observed friction
- source receipts
- proposed change
- why this improves locality, leverage, and tests
- conflict with existing Brain/ADR decisions, if any
- risk and first reversible step

Do not jump straight into implementation. Ask which candidate to explore unless Joel explicitly asked for a concrete change.

## SVX Capture

Architecture reviews should usually leave a Brain receipt:

- `.brain/resources/<repo>-architecture-review.svx` for review findings
- `.brain/projects/<project>.svx` for active implementation plan updates
- `.brain/resources/decisions/<slug>.svx` or repo ADRs for hard-to-reverse decisions
- domain term updates in project Brain Area/Resource notes when language is resolved; do not extend `CONTEXT.md` unless explicit repo policy requires it

Use `.svx` frontmatter, source receipts, and links to code paths. Run `pi-notes brain check` after Brain edits when available.

## Rule

If Joel rejects a recurring architecture suggestion for a durable reason, offer to capture it as a decision so future agents stop re-suggesting the same bullshit.

# Joel's Writing Style Guide

Joel writes like he talks — direct, warm, profane when it serves the point, and always in service of helping someone. His blog is a digital garden, not a content marketing operation. Posts range from 50-word observations to 4,000-word deep dives. Not everything is polished. That's by design.

This guide is derived from analyzing 127 posts across joelhooks.com (2012–2026).

For curated voice examples from the corpus, see [references/voice-examples.md](references/voice-examples.md).

---

## Core Voice Rules

### 1. Write conversationally in first person

Address the reader as "you." Use "I" and "we" freely. Write like you're explaining something to a smart friend over coffee — not like you're writing a blog post.

- Contractions always: it's, doesn't, I've, they're, we've, can't, won't
- Never stilted: "one might consider" → "you might try"
- No "Dear reader" or "In this post I will" throat-clearing

### 2. Strategic profanity is texture, not shock

Joel uses "fuck," "shit," "bullshit," "damn," and "af" naturally when they serve emphasis. Average 3–5 instances per substantive post. They land because they're infrequent enough to carry weight.

**When to use it:**
- Emphasis on a point: "I'm convinced that paginated posted sorted chronologically fuckin' sucks."
- Dismissing bad ideas: "No 'growth hacks' or other bullshit involved"
- Raw honesty: "I'm a shit PM."
- Celebration: "holy shit, feels good."

**When NOT to use it:**
- Never in headlines or H2s (rare exception: "Just Fucking Do It" as a deliberate title)
- Never gratuitously — if removing it doesn't weaken the sentence, remove it
- Never to be edgy — it should feel natural, like breathing

### 3. Short paragraphs, punchy rhythm

Most paragraphs are 1–3 sentences. Many are single-sentence paragraphs for emphasis. Alternate short and long sentences to create rhythm.

**The pattern:** Short. Short. Longer sentence that develops the idea with some texture and detail. Short punch.

This creates a reading experience that pulls you down the page.

### 4. Bold for inline emphasis, not decoration

Use **bold** to punch key phrases within sentences. Not for headers-within-paragraphs. Not for every other word.

- ✅ "We provide instructors with a **world class highly skilled production team that they don't have to fuckin manage**."
- ✅ "If it's negotiable, you'll negotiate your way out."
- ❌ Bolding entire sentences or paragraphs
- ❌ Using bold as a substitute for good writing

### 5. Emoji as warmth, not decoration

Joel uses emoji sparingly — ❤️ 🤯 😅 😂 🔥 🥰 — often at paragraph endings. They convey genuine emotion. Never more than 2–3 per post.

- ✅ "Thanks to Marie Poulin for this idea ❤️"
- ✅ "That's when I started working on egghead.io which is what I've been doing for 6 years. 🔥"
- ❌ Emoji in every paragraph
- ❌ Emoji as bullet points or list markers (except occasionally in titles: "🌱 My blog is a digital garden")

### 6. Italics for internal voice and refrains

Use *italics* for thoughts, recurring questions, and emphasis that's softer than bold.

- *"What would happen if I did this for a year?"*
- *badass web developer* (as a concept/identity)
- _just don't feel like doing the activities required to make more money_

## Structural Patterns

### Never lead with a heading

The title is already an H1 rendered above the content. An `## H2` as the first line of the body looks redundant and amateurish — two headings stacked with nothing between them. Always open with prose: a hook, a sentence, an observation. The heading comes after the opening paragraph or after any install/code block at the top.

- ❌ `## The interface is stdout` (right after title — two headings in a row)
- ✅ A prose sentence, then `## The interface is stdout` further down
- ✅ A skill install code block, then prose, then the first heading

### Opening hooks, not thesis statements

Never open with "In this article, I'll discuss..." — open with a hook that creates tension, asks a question, or drops you into a moment.

**Strong openings from Joel's corpus:**
- "290 pounds and I couldn't walk and talk at the same time."
- "Have you used Jira?"
- "Recording a podcast is a shitload of work."
- "Most personal AI projects start with a database."
- "We crossed the $16M milestone on 2019-12-05."
- "Being able to work remotely is probably one of the coolest fuckin things that's ever happened to me."

**⚠️ These are examples, not templates.** Do NOT copy a hook's structure and swap the nouns — "Most personal AI projects start with a chat window" is just "Most personal AI projects start with a database" wearing a fake mustache. Every hook should be **original to the piece**. The pattern is "create tension or drop into a moment," not "Most X start with Y, but I did Z." If you catch yourself writing a comparison frame as a hook ("Most people do X / Unlike typical Y / The standard approach is Z"), throw it out. Start with the thing itself — what it does, why it matters, what broke.

### Headers as narrative beats

Headers tell a story, not an outline. They're conversational, sometimes sentence fragments.

- ✅ "## I quit my job." / "## The Commitment Problem" / "## Finding My Place"
- ✅ "## We are not a commodity." / "## The bet"
- ❌ "## Introduction" / "## Key Takeaways" / "## Conclusion"

### Endings are often abrupt

No forced wrap-up or "In conclusion..." — just stop when the idea is done. Often a short, warm line.

- "Life is good."
- "Bring it New Year."
- "I'm excited to find out."
- "It's very exciting, and I look forward to exploring this idea more."

### Variable post length is intentional

The digital garden philosophy means a post can be 50 words or 4,000. A "Barber Shop Paradox" post that's three sentences is just as valid as a deep-dive book review. Don't pad short ideas to fill space.

### Links woven into narrative

Never "click here." Links are part of the sentence flow.

- ✅ "I highly recommend watching [this video from Jay Abraham](url)."
- ✅ "We partnered with [Dan Abramov and Maggie Appleton](url) to help produce their online course."
- ❌ "[Click here](url) to learn more."

### Tables for comparison, not decoration

Joel uses tables when making architectural comparisons or showing before/after. Keep them focused.

---

## Philosophical DNA

These values permeate Joel's writing. Content that contradicts them will feel off-voice regardless of surface-level style matching.

### User outcomes over features
"Don't make a better tutorial video. Make a better frontend web developer." Every piece connects technology or process to human outcomes.

### Clients, not customers
From Jay Abraham's Strategy of Preeminence: "A client is someone who is under the care & protection of another." Joel treats readers as people he's advising, not audiences he's monetizing.

### Anti-performative
The blog is for Joel first, readers second. "It's not that I don't care about you, but this is for me." This honesty paradoxically makes it more valuable to readers.

### JFDI (Just Fucking Do It)
Bias toward action. "Quitting is a habit too — and I'm not training that one." No hand-wringing. Decide, commit, iterate.

### Consistency > perfection
"Imperfection doesn't mean failure — stopping does." Posts can be seedlings. Ideas can be half-formed. Ship it and tend the garden.

### Sovereignty and ownership
Self-host. Own your data. Own your platform. Against dependence on platforms that can be ruined by "one asshole."

### Crediting sources
Always name people and link to their work. Alex Hillman, Amy Hoy, Kathy Sierra, Tiago Forte, Jay Abraham — the network of thinkers is visible.

---

## The Fabrication Rule — NEVER Make Things Up

**This is the single most important rule in this skill.**

When writing in Joel's voice, you are putting words in a real person's mouth. Every claim, anecdote, experience, and opinion must be **verifiably true** or **explicitly flagged as a placeholder for Joel to fill in**.

### What counts as fabrication:
- Inventing personal anecdotes Joel never lived ("I tried X for a week and it broke")
- Claiming specific experiences ("here's what happened in my last 24 hours")
- Putting opinions in Joel's mouth that he never expressed
- Fabricating conversations, reactions, or emotional responses
- Inventing links to posts or resources that don't exist
- Making up metrics, timelines, or results
- **Guessing temporal facts instead of looking them up.** If the text says "a couple of weeks" and you don't know the actual timeframe, LOOK IT UP in git history, slog, or ADRs. Never substitute one guess for another ("weeks" → "months"). Temporal claims must be verified against source data or flagged as `[TODO: verify timeframe]`.
- Writing endorsements or testimonials Joel never gave

### What to do instead:
- **Describe the system factually.** "The pipeline does X" not "I spent three days building X and here's what I learned"
- **Use verifiable facts.** Read the actual code, configs, logs, and git history. Cite what's real.
- **Flag gaps honestly.** If you don't know Joel's opinion on something, write `[TODO: Joel's take on X]` — don't guess.
- **Attribute the source.** If an architectural detail comes from an ADR or code comment, that's a fact. If you're inferring Joel's feelings about it, that's fabrication.
- **Stick to third-person for uncertain claims.** "The system does X" is always safe. "I love how X works" requires Joel to have actually said that.

### Pontification must come from Joel

If a passage expresses *how Joel thinks*, *what Joel believes*, or *Joel's philosophy* about a topic — it **must be sourced from Joel's actual words** (conversations, vault notes, past writing, direct quotes). An LLM cannot generate philosophical positions, hot takes, or worldview statements and attribute them to Joel. These are the highest-trust sentences in any article.

- ❌ "I think it is. Not because the metaphor is precise, but because it's *useful*." (LLM inventing Joel's philosophical stance)
- ❌ "The question is whether 'alive' is the right frame..." (LLM constructing Joel's intellectual framing)
- ✅ Describe what the system does factually, then `[TODO: Joel's take on what this means]`
- ✅ Quote Joel directly from a conversation or past writing
- ✅ Joel writes the closing himself via feedback

When in doubt: **end the article before the pontification.** A factual ending that stops when the idea is done is infinitely better than an AI-generated philosophical flourish pretending to be Joel's inner monologue.

Writing in someone's voice is a privilege. The moment you invent experiences they never had, you're not writing *for* them — you're putting words in their mouth. That's not a style problem. That's a trust problem.

---

## Anti-Patterns — What Joel Never Does

| Never | Instead |
|---|---|
| "Leverage," "utilize," "synergize," "facilitate" | "Use," "help," "make" |
| "In this post, I will explore..." | Jump straight into the hook |
| Passive voice: "Mistakes were made" | Active: "I fucked that up" |
| Clickbait titles | Direct, sometimes playful, never misleading |
| Exclamation point spam!!!! | Rare. Maybe one per post. Let the words do the work. |
| "Key takeaways" / "TL;DR" sections | Reader can handle the full piece or skim naturally |
| Hedging: "I think maybe perhaps" | Say it: "This is how it works." |
| Generic "content marketing" voice | Specific, personal, opinionated |
| Hiding behind "we" when he means "I" | "I" for personal opinions, "we" for team efforts (egghead) |
| SEO keyword stuffing | Write for humans. Search follows substance. |
| Attribution-free idea theft | Names and links for every borrowed concept |
| "Let me be real" intros | Just be real without announcing it |
| "What I Actually Built" | "What I Built" — no need to emphasize actuality |
| Calling things "dumb" when you mean "unnatural" | Be precise about the actual friction |
| "Genuinely useful" | "Useful" — the adverb adds nothing |
| "as hell" intensifier | Just "rough" is stronger than "rough as hell" |
| Making up kids' reactions | They "didn't give a fuck" not "saw it as dial-up" |
| "real power" | Say what it actually does |
| "wake-up call" | Just state the fact |
| "fundamentally changes" | "Changes" — if it's fundamental, show it |
| "key benefit" / "key insight" | Just state the benefit/insight |
| "cut through the noise" | Say what it does specifically |
| "the irony" | Show the irony, don't label it |
| "the good news" / "the reality" | Just say the thing |
| "it's kind of like" | Use a direct metaphor or don't |
| "here's the thing:" | Just say the thing |
| "hard truth" / "uncomfortable truth" | State it. If it's hard, the reader will feel it |

---

## Content Types on joelclaw.com

The blog is a serialized book about building a personal AI operating system. Content falls into these patterns:

### Architecture deep-dives
Technical decisions explained with clear tables, rationale, and "the bet" framing. See: "AT Protocol as Bedrock," "Why I Built My Own AI System."

- Lead with the question that prompted the decision
- Use comparison tables for architecture choices
- End with honest assessment of tradeoffs ("That's a bet.")

### Personal essays
Stories from Joel's life that connect to broader lessons. See: "Getting Jacked at 50," "Setting Goals for My Version of Success."

- Open with a vivid moment, not a thesis
- Use chronological narrative with section headers as story beats
- Let the lesson emerge from the story — don't moralize at the end

### Tool/system reviews
Honest assessments of tools, gear, books. See: "Badass: Making Users Awesome," "Self-Hosting."

- Lead with why it matters, not what it is
- Include personal experience and context
- Recommend genuinely — Joel doesn't do lukewarm reviews

### Business philosophy
Frameworks and principles. See: "Strategy of Preeminence," "Making Other People Money."

- Ground abstract principles in specific egghead/joelclaw experience
- Use Jay Abraham and Kathy Sierra as philosophical touchstones
- Connect back to "making other people successful" as the core thesis

### Short observations
Digital garden seedlings — a single idea in a few sentences. See: "The Barber Shop Paradox," "Write for somebody specific."

- Don't pad. If the idea is three sentences, publish three sentences.
- These can grow later. That's the garden.

---

## Voice Calibration Checklist

Before publishing, run this pass:

- [ ] Does it sound like Joel talking, or like an AI writing "casually"?
- [ ] Is there at least one moment of raw honesty?
- [ ] Are paragraphs mostly 1–3 sentences?
- [ ] Does it open with a hook, not a preamble?
- [ ] Is profanity (if present) earning its keep?
- [ ] Are people credited by name?
- [ ] Does it connect to a human outcome, not just a technical fact?
- [ ] Is the ending natural, not forced?
- [ ] Would Joel actually publish this on his site?
- [ ] Is every claim, anecdote, and experience **verifiably true**? (No fabricated stories, fake metrics, or invented opinions)
- [ ] Are there `[TODO]` placeholders for anything you're uncertain Joel would say?

The fabrication check is the one that truly matters. Everything else is style. Getting the facts wrong is a trust violation.

# Prototype

A prototype is throwaway code that answers one question. The answer is the artifact worth keeping.

## Pick The Branch

Identify the question:

- Logic/state/data model question → tiny interactive terminal app or focused harness.
- UI/design question → several radically different variants switchable from one route.

If finite modes, retries, cancellation, resumability, workflow status, or child processes are involved, sketch an explicit XState v5 machine before implementation. Boolean soup is where future bugs hatch.

## Rules For Both Branches

- Mark prototype code clearly as throwaway.
- Put it close to the real module/page so context is obvious.
- One command or URL to run.
- No persistence unless persistence is the thing being tested.
- Surface the current state after every action or variant change.
- No production polish, broad abstractions, or test suites for the throwaway shell.
- Delete or absorb when done.

## Logic Prototype

Use the host project's runtime. Keep logic portable behind a small pure interface:

- reducer
- state machine
- pure functions over a plain data type
- small module/class only when it genuinely owns state

The TUI/harness is disposable. The reducer/machine/function shape may be the reusable part.

## UI Prototype

Prefer variants inside an existing route so they are judged against real app chrome, data, density, and auth.

Use `?variant=` or the framework's equivalent so variants are shareable and reload-stable. Variants must differ structurally, not just color/copy. Hide prototype switchers in production builds.

## SVX Capture

Before or during the prototype, record the question in the active Brain note:

```txt
.brain/projects/<slug>.svx
```

When done, capture:

- question answered
- winning decision or rejected path
- why it won/failed
- run command or URL used
- files to delete or absorb
- follow-up implementation issue, if any

Use project-local `.svx` first. Use `~/.brain` only for cross-project/operator learning. Treat `CONTEXT.md`-style files as legacy evidence, not prototype result storage. Run `pi-notes brain check .` after Brain edits when available.

## Anti-Patterns

- leaving prototype routes/components to rot
- wiring throwaway UI to real mutations
- making variants that are just three card grids with different hats
- promoting prototype code directly to production without rewriting the production version
- keeping the prototype but losing the answer

# Test-Driven Development

TDD here means one behavior at a time through the public interface. Not "write a pile of imagined tests and then bully the code until green."

## Philosophy

Good tests verify behavior through public interfaces. Code can change entirely; tests should survive.

Bad tests couple to implementation: private methods, internal collaborators, call counts, or database peeking when the public interface can verify the behavior.

Mock only at system boundaries: external APIs, time/randomness, filesystem when needed, and sometimes databases when a local stand-in is unavailable. Do not mock your own modules just because setup is annoying.

## Before Writing Code

Inspect:

- relevant code/tests/config
- project `.brain/**/*.svx` through pi-notes when present, plus `~/.brain` for cross-project/operator context
- ADRs and domain docs as evidence; legacy `BRAIN.md`/`CONTEXT.md` only as migration inputs
- existing test patterns and commands

Confirm or infer:

- public interface to exercise
- critical behaviors to test first
- non-goals
- validation command
- whether a missing seam is the real problem

If interface/test decisions are durable architecture, capture them in the active `.svx` PRD/project note or a decision note. Do not record every tiny red/green step; capture only decisions future agents need.

## Red → Green → Refactor

Vertical tracer bullets only:

1. Write one failing test for one behavior.
2. Run it and confirm the expected failure.
3. Write minimal code to pass.
4. Run focused tests.
5. Repeat for the next behavior.
6. Refactor only when green.
7. Run the validation contract.

Never refactor while red. Never add speculative behavior for future tests.

## Deep Module Discipline

Look for modules with small interfaces and useful depth. The interface is the test surface. If tests need to reach past the interface, the module shape may be wrong.

If the implementation reveals no good test seam, document that as an architecture finding in Brain/project notes after the immediate work is safe.

## SVX Capture

Use `.svx` for durable outcomes:

- `.brain/projects/<slug>.svx` — tested behaviors, validation contract, accepted interface decisions
- `.brain/resources/<slug>.svx` — reusable testing patterns or bug class receipts
- `.brain/resources/decisions/<slug>.svx` — hard-to-reverse interface/seam choices

Run `pi-notes brain check .` after Brain edits when available.

## Per-Cycle Checklist

- test describes behavior, not implementation
- test uses public interface only
- failure proves the right thing
- code is minimal for this test
- no speculative features
- debug/prototype junk cleaned up

# Write A Skill

Skills are generated from local truth, not copied from upstream. Upstream skills are design inputs. Finished skills must fit Joel's machine, Brain, pi-notes, and public/private boundaries.

Figure out where the user is in the skill lifecycle, then jump in there. They may be starting from a vague workflow, adapting an upstream skill, editing an existing local skill, testing behavior, improving trigger accuracy, or packaging something for reuse. Do not force the full eval loop when Joel asks for a small repair, but do preserve the option when the skill is meant to be reused a lot.

## System Prompt Extraction

Use this split when gardening prompts:

- system prompt = familiar contract, hard safety, model/tool boundaries, durable operator taste
- skills = detailed runbooks, niche workflows, product playbooks, commands, examples, and reference-heavy doctrine

Do not shrink the voice out of the prompt. Extract cold detail into a trigger-rich skill only when it reduces always-on prompt load or fixes trigger noise.

## Source Pass

Before writing:

- read the upstream/source skill if adapting one
- inspect existing local skills with the same trigger
- search Brain or bounded session history when the workflow came from repeated friction
- extract intent from the current conversation before asking the user to repeat themselves
- identify public/private boundary and install consumers
- decide whether the task is creation, existing-skill update, eval/iteration, trigger-description optimization, or packaging
- choose the owning source repo:
  - `dark-wizard/skills` for private operator, Brain, session, Panda, or pi-notes behavior
  - `joelclaw/skills` for JoelClaw runtime/system behavior
  - project repo for project-specific skills
  - domain repo (`badass-courses`, support, etc.) for domain doctrine

Do not make `dark-wizard` a junk drawer. Use it for personal/operator adaptations, not every useful skill on earth.

## Skill Shape

Keep `SKILL.md` concise:

- frontmatter `name`, trigger-rich `description`, and `basis:` when forked
- descriptions should be a little pushy because skills under-trigger, include specific user phrases, adjacent contexts, and when this skill should win
- put all trigger guidance in the description, not buried in the body
- local source-of-truth order
- workflow steps
- expected output format when stable
- real commands for this machine only
- safety/privacy rules
- references/scripts only when the main file would get too long

Use progressive disclosure:

1. metadata is always visible, so keep `description` accurate and high-signal
2. `SKILL.md` should stay under roughly 500 lines when practical
3. bundled `scripts/`, `references/`, and `assets/` hold repeatable machinery and bulky docs

If several test runs or past sessions reinvent the same helper script, bundle it in `scripts/` and tell the skill when to use it. Repeated reinvention is a receipt, not a vibe.

## Intent Capture

When creating or substantially changing a skill, capture enough intent before editing:

1. What should the skill enable the agent to do?
2. When should it trigger, including casual phrases and near-miss cases?
3. What output should the user receive?
4. Are test cases worth it? Use evals for repeatable transforms, deterministic workflows, code generation, or costly high-use skills. Skip formal evals for tiny fixes and subjective taste unless Joel asks.

Ask only for missing information. If the conversation already contains the workflow, extract it and confirm the summary.

## Practical Eval Loop

Use the Anthropic eval loop when the skill is important enough to justify it:

1. write 2 to 3 realistic prompts in `evals/evals.json`
2. for a new skill, compare with-skill against no-skill baseline
3. for an existing skill, snapshot the old version and compare against the edited version
4. save outputs under a sibling workspace like `<skill-name>-workspace/iteration-1/`
5. grade objective assertions with scripts or a reviewer, and keep subjective feedback human-readable
6. show the user outputs before overfitting the skill
7. revise the skill, rerun, and stop when feedback is clean or progress stalls

In Pi, prefer `subagent` for with-skill and baseline runs when available. If the harness lacks browser or reviewer tooling, use a static HTML report or a concise inline review instead of building a custom platform. Do not use Anthropic-specific commands blindly unless the repo actually includes those scripts.

## Trigger Description Optimization

After creating or heavily improving a reusable skill, offer to tune the description. A good trigger eval set has realistic prompts, not toy keywords:

- 8 to 10 should-trigger prompts with varied phrasing, typos, and implicit intent
- 8 to 10 should-not-trigger near misses that share words but need another skill or normal tools
- substantive tasks, because one-step requests may not trigger skills even with a perfect description

Apply the best description only after reviewing false positives and false negatives. Preserve the skill `name` when updating an existing skill.

## Existing Skill Updates

When updating an installed skill:

- preserve the directory name and frontmatter `name`
- snapshot the old version if you are doing formal evals
- edit the canonical source, not a consumer symlink, unless the canonical source is intentionally unavailable
- avoid renaming into `*-v2` sludge
- package from a writable copy only when the installed location is read-only

## SVX / Brain Compatibility

If the skill encodes durable behavior, capture the decision in Brain as `.svx`:

```md

title: "Short Human Title"
type: "resource"
status: "active"
created_at: "YYYY-MM-DD"
tags:
  - agent-skills
---

# Short Human Title

Source receipts, decision, and operating rules.
```

Prefer:

- `.brain/projects/*.svx` for active outcomes and PRDs
- `.brain/areas/*.svx` for durable responsibilities
- `.brain/resources/*.svx` for reusable references, source maps, and review receipts
- `.brain/resources/decisions/*.svx` or project ADR location for hard-to-reverse decisions

Use project-local Brain first. Use `~/.brain` for cross-project/machine/operator knowledge. Run `pi-notes brain check` after Brain edits when available.

## Install Wiring

For machine-wide skills, update the dotfiles catalog/manifest when the install should be repeatable:

- `/Users/joel/Code/joelhooks/dotfiles/docs/agent-skills.md`
- `/Users/joel/Code/joelhooks/dotfiles/manifests/agent-skill-roots.tsv`
